newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada opens local phone market to competition.
newsitem.headline: Canada opens local phone market to competition.

text.p: Canada's communications regulatory agency on Thursday threw the country's local telephone market open to competition while also promoting convergence between the phone and cable television broadcast businesses.

A complex set of decisions by the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) also approved a C$3 ($2.19) a month increase in local phone charges effective on Jan. 1 and a price cap formula to apply to services thereafter.

The decisions, which can be appealed to the federal cabinet, opened Canada's C$8 billion ($6 billion) local phone market to competition immediately and said phone companies would be allowed to apply to begin broadcast distribution in 1998.

Under the new rules, cable televison companies, including Canada's two biggest, Toronto-based Rogers Communications Inc.'s Rogers Cablesystems and Groupe Videotron Ltee., of Montreal, will be allowed to offer local telephone services immediately.
At a press conference, CRTC Chairwoman Francoise Bertrand said the new regulations were a crucial part of the continuing development of Canada's telecommunications industry.
"We want our country to be part of an information highway by which we have enchanced services," Bertrand said.

The new competition rules came five years after the CRTC allowed foreign and domestic companies into the country's lucrative long-distance telephone market, which had been the reserve of domestic providers of local services such as BCE Inc.'s Bell Canada unit, Canada's largest telephone company.
That provoked a restructuring at Bell during which it will have cut 10,000 jobs by the end of this year.

In a significant deviation from the controversial deregulation route taken in the United States, the CRTC denied a request by companies such as Sprint Corp. that Bell Canada and other established companies be forced to sell local services at wholesale rates.
Bertrand said the rationale there was to force new entrants to build new telecommunications infrastructure rather than merely buy services wholesale to resell them.

Independent telecommunications analyst Ian Angus said Canada's Stentor alliance of established phone companies, which includes Bell Canada and BC Telecom Inc., would not be entirely displeased with the new rules.
"I would say the Stentor companies won more than they lost," he said.
In a statement, Bell Canada President John McLennan reserved judgment on the new CRTC rules, but said the company supports "fair and open competition in all aspects of our business."

Bob Simmonds, chairman of Toronto-based Clearnet Communications Inc., a wireless telecom company whose major shareholders include Motorola Inc. and Nextel Communications Inc., said he welcomed the CRTC rules.
"It's a really excellent decision. It eliminates a lot of the barriers to entering the local market," he said.
